shinyOAuthDB lets Shiny visitors query data using their own database or
platform account. Use it when the data each person may access should follow
their database permissions.

Choose your source below. Each guide includes its sign-in setup and a
complete Shiny app, followed by examples for working with your data.

## Choose your source

| Source | What the guide covers |
| --- | --- |
| [Azure SQL and SQL Server](azure-sql.html) | Entra sign-in, DBI, and dbplyr |
| [Microsoft Fabric](fabric.html) | SQL endpoints, fabricQueryR functions, and resource objects |
| [Databricks](databricks.html) | SQL warehouses and brickster API calls |
| [Snowflake](snowflake.html) | Snowflake OAuth, roles, and DBI queries |
| [Google BigQuery](bigquery.html) | Google sign-in and GoogleSQL queries returning data frames |
| [Amazon Redshift](redshift.html) | Delegated user tokens through the AWS ODBC driver |
| [Trino and Starburst Enterprise](trino.html) | OIDC sign-in and RTrino DBI queries |
| [Azure PostgreSQL](azure-postgres.html) | Entra sign-in and RPostgres connections |

## Install the package

shinyOAuthDB is available from GitHub:

```{r installation}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lukakoning/shinyOAuthDB")
```

This installs shinyOAuth too. Some sources also need an R client and a
system database driver; the source guide tells you which ones.

## Sign-in and data access

Register an OAuth application with the source's identity provider. The
registration gives your Shiny app a client ID and, for a confidential app,
a client secret. It also sets the redirect URI, where the browser returns
after sign-in. The example apps use `http://localhost:8100`.

You don't need an existing shinyOAuth configuration. Each source guide
creates the appropriate client, and uses shinyOAuth's UI and server module
to let visitors sign in. The user also needs permission to read the data;
registering an app or granting OAuth consent doesn't provide database access.

Create the sign-in client outside `server()`. Inside `server()`, pass
`auth$connection` to a database helper or API client. This keeps data access
in the visitor's Shiny session and follows their sign-in changes.

With a DBI helper, call `connection <- con()` inside a render or reactive
expression before querying. You can then use ordinary DBI or dbplyr calls.
The helper opens and reuses the connection, then closes it when the
authorization or Shiny session ends. API clients provide query methods or
call the source's R functions with the visitor's credentials.

## Adapt an example

Start with your source's complete app and replace its example connection
settings and query. Save credentials in a local `.Renviron` file as shown
in the guide, restart R, then run `shiny::runApp(port = 8100)` from the app
directory. Keep the app's URL and registered redirect URI consistent.

For an existing login, several accounts, or results saved between button
clicks, continue with [Authentication and sessions](authorization.html).
